overview: This bill would require the Labor Department's Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA), which enforces federal rules for workplace retirement and health plans, to send Congress a yearly report on its investigations. For each case, the report would list which office opened it, when it started, and when the agency first asked for documents. If an investigation has gone on more than 36 months past that first request, the report must explain why and give an expected end date. The report could not name any private party, such as employers, plan managers, service providers or workers. The House Education and Workforce Committee approved an amended version, and it was placed on the House calendar on February 10, 2026.
for: Supporters say some investigations drag on for years, and regular reporting would help Congress spot delays and hold the agency accountable while protecting the privacy of those involved.
against: Critics say the reporting work could pull staff away from investigations, and public tracking of case timelines might pressure the agency to close complex cases early.
